author: blu
body: LZ77 compression and decompression. Encodes repeated byte sequences as back-references (offset, length). Window size 32768, max match 258. Token format: 0 + literal byte, or 1 + offset + length for a match.

author: blu
body: The window was 255 bytes and the longest match 255, which was not a format limit anywhere -- RFC 1951 permits 32768 and 258, and Brotli permits far more. It was the limit of a brute-force scan: every position compared against every earlier position in the window, so widening the window multiplied the work by the same factor. At 32768 that scan is a hundred and twenty-eight times slower and simply cannot be run.

author: blu
body: So the search changed shape before the window could grow. Positions are indexed by a hash of the three bytes starting there, and the candidates for a position are the chain of earlier positions with the same hash, walked newest first. The window is now a bound on the chain rather than a range to sweep, and the cost stops depending on it.

author: blu
body: The cap is now a parameter of the search, and this constant is what Deflate's own callers pass. Raising the constant instead would have been shorter and would have emitted invalid Deflate, which nothing in the tree can currently catch: Deflate's oracle harness was deleted with the compression stack.

author: blu
body: The hash is over three bytes, which is the shortest match worth taking. Sixteen thousand buckets against a window of thirty-two thousand keeps chains short without spending a slot per position, and collisions cost only a wasted comparison because the bytes are checked anyway.

author: blu
body: A match costs a length code and a distance code, and a distant one costs more distance bits. A literal costs whatever the entropy coder charges for it. Those two prices decide whether a match is worth taking at all, and a greedy matcher that takes every match it finds is answering that question without asking it.

author: blu
body: So the matcher estimates both prices. The literal price is taken once per tokenization from how many distinct bytes the input uses -- a crude proxy for its entropy, but the right shape and nearly free. The match price is the twelve-odd bits of length and distance codes plus a bit per doubling of the distance. A match is taken when it plausibly saves.

author: blu
body: It is an ESTIMATE and it is allowed to be wrong: being wrong costs ratio, the same as any other thing the chain guesses at. What it cannot do is make the output invalid, so it is safe to keep crude.

author: blu
body: Two tables. head holds, for each hash, the most recent position that started there; prev holds, for each position modulo the window, the position that head pointed at when this one was inserted. Following prev from head therefore walks the positions sharing a hash, newest first, and a position falls out of reach on its own once the window has wrapped past it.

author: blu
body: A position with fewer than three bytes left cannot start a match, and says so with a negative hash rather than reading past the end.

author: blu
body: Every position a match covers is indexed too, not just the one it starts at. A match consumes several positions at once, and leaving them out of the chains costs later positions the matches that would have started inside it.

author: blu
body: THE PRICE ONLY MAKES SENSE FOR AN ENTROPY-CODED CONSUMER. Lz77's own token format is not one: a literal costs a tag and a byte, two slots, while a match costs three whatever its length or distance. A match of the minimum length already replaces six slots with three, so every match this chapter finds is worth taking and there is no decision to make. Handing the estimate a literal price nothing can outbid says exactly that.

author: blu
body: Measured the hard way: pricing this chapter's own output as if literals were four bits made a nine-byte input compress to eighteen slots instead of nine, because a three-symbol alphabet reads as one bit per literal and no match can beat that. The prices are Deflate's and Brotli's, not this format's.

author: blu
body: How many bits a literal is worth, guessed from the size of the alphabet the input uses. Two distinct bytes is one bit, sixteen is four, a full byte range is eight.

author: blu
body: Recomputing every lz77-est-window bytes costs one pass over the input in total, since each recompute walks its own chunk once and the chunks do not overlap.

author: blu
body: Lazy matching, which is the other thing a greedy scan gets wrong. Taking a match the moment one is found forecloses a longer one starting one byte later, and the longer one is usually worth more than the literal it costs to wait. So a match that is not already the longest possible looks at what the next position would find, and yields to it.

author: blu
body: The next position is searched WITHOUT this one having been inserted, so it sees a slightly smaller candidate set than it will when its turn comes. That is the chain being a hint again: the comparison is a little conservative and never wrong.
